title: People Are Animals and Hidden Meanings
tagline: character, secrets and things nobody says
why: English uses animals to judge people quickly and indirectly: a lone wolf, the black sheep, crocodile tears. Many of these idioms also name what is hidden or unspoken, so they are essential for reading between the lines.
know: eight key idioms such as the elephant in the room, a red herring and a dark horse
everyday hidden animal verbs: wolf down, badger, weasel out of, ferret out, parrot
understand: that each animal carries a fixed character in English, which may differ from your own language
that animal labels judge people, so they can sound insulting or humorous
able: describe people's character and roles with the right animal idiom
talk about secrets, distractions and awkward truths indirectly
discuss fables, novels and poems that use animals as metaphors
mistakes: She let the dog out of the bag.
She let the cat out of the bag. The animal is fixed.
He shed crocodile tears. Crocodile works as an adjective, before the noun.
The boss took the share of the lion.
The boss took the lion's share. Use the possessive, not of the.
There's an elephant in the room: by the way, how was your holiday?
Use it only for a serious, avoided problem, then actually name or address it.
My brother is the black sheep: he's a doctor and everyone's proud of him.
The black sheep is the family member seen as a disappointment, not just someone different.
bigidea: People are often described as animals, and each animal carries a fixed character: foxes are cunning, wolves are dangerous or solitary, sheep follow the crowd, lions are powerful. Most of these images come from fables, farming and the Bible, so they are old and stable.

A second group is about hidden meaning: secrets kept in bags, enormous animals nobody mentions, smelly fish that lead you off the trail. These idioms let speakers point at awkward truths without saying them directly.

Because animal labels judge character, they are rarely neutral. Calling a colleague a snake or a politician a dinosaur is a strong move. Check whether the animal means the same thing in your language: an owl is wise in English but unlucky in some cultures.
hidden: He wolfed down his lunch in five minutes.
The senator weaselled out of answering the question.
She's been hounded by reporters all week.
Don't just parrot the textbook; give your own view.
The journalist ferreted out the truth from old tax records.
A few sheepish employees admitted they hadn't read the policy.

expressions.meaning: an obvious, important problem that everyone avoids mentioning
expressions.example: Nobody at the family dinner mentioned Dad's drinking, but it was the elephant in the room.
expressions.bend: Flexible: address the elephant in the room, a huge elephant in the room, even a whole herd of elephants as a joke.
expressions.note: Very common in business and politics, so some editors call it overused. Address or acknowledge the elephant is the usual verb.

expressions.meaning: something that distracts attention from the real issue, often deliberately
expressions.example: The fuss about the mayor's haircut was a red herring; the real issue was the budget.
expressions.bend: Fixed noun phrase, but plurals work: the novel is full of red herrings.
expressions.note: A favourite term in mystery fiction for a false clue. Its exact origin is debated, so treat the popular dog-training story with caution.

expressions.meaning: a little-known competitor who unexpectedly succeeds, or someone with surprising hidden talents
expressions.example: Nobody expected the quiet candidate from Saskatchewan to win; she was a dark horse.
expressions.bend: Used as an adjective: a dark-horse candidate. British speakers also say You're a dark horse! to someone with a surprising secret.
expressions.note: Popularised by Benjamin Disraeli's novel The Young Duke (1831), in which an unknown horse wins a race. Never black horse.

expressions.e: let the cat out of the bag
expressions.meaning: reveal a secret, usually by accident
expressions.example: My nephew let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
expressions.bend: Flexible: the cat's out of the bag now, who let the cat out?
expressions.note: Usually accidental. For a deliberate leak to the press, leak or blow the whistle is more precise.

expressions.example: The province's two largest cities receive the lion's share of the funding.
expressions.bend: Almost fixed: the lion's share of. Singular lion, with an apostrophe before the s.
expressions.note: From an Aesop fable in which the lion keeps all the prey for himself. Originally it meant all of it; today it usually means the biggest part.

expressions.meaning: a belief, custom or institution treated as beyond criticism
expressions.example: The new CEO says no department is a sacred cow in the budget review.
expressions.bend: Plurals are common: challenge sacred cows, slaughter a few sacred cows.
expressions.note: Inspired by the reverence for cows in Hinduism. Used about politics and business; be thoughtful using it in conversations about religion itself.

expressions.example: The executives shed crocodile tears over the layoffs while accepting huge bonuses.
expressions.bend: Usually with shed or weep: shedding crocodile tears. Always plural.
expressions.note: From an old legend that crocodiles weep while eating their prey. It is a strong accusation of hypocrisy.

expressions.meaning: a dangerous person who appears harmless
expressions.example: The friendly investment adviser turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing.
expressions.bend: Plural works: wolves in sheep's clothing. The rest is fixed.
expressions.note: The image appears in the Gospel of Matthew, warning against false prophets, and in later fables attributed to Aesop.

culture.how: Short stories in which animals behave like people: a lion who keeps all the prey, a wolf disguised in a fleece, a fox who calls the grapes he can't reach sour. Each animal is a fixed human type, and English inherited idioms such as the lion's share and sour grapes from them.
culture.ask: Is there a fable or folk tale from your culture whose moral became a common saying?

culture.how: Farm animals overthrow their human farmer, but the pigs slowly become new tyrants. The whole novel is an extended metaphor, an allegory, for the Russian Revolution and Stalin's rule, with each animal standing for a type of person or group.
culture.ask: Why might a writer tell a political story with animals instead of people? What does it allow him to say?

culture.work: Hope is the thing with feathers
culture.how: Dickinson pictures hope as a small bird living inside a person, singing without stopping through the worst storms and never asking for anything in return. An abstract feeling becomes a creature you can almost hold.
culture.ask: If you described courage, worry or love as an animal, which animal would it be?
culture.find: Emily Dickinson Hope is the thing with feathers

culture.how: The singer describes moving from being quiet and pushed around to finding her strength. The tiger and its roar become a metaphor for confidence regained, a modern pop version of the lion as a symbol of courage.
culture.ask: Which animal would you choose as a symbol of confidence in your culture? Is it the same as in English?

culture.how: A travelling salesman wakes up transformed into a huge insect, and his family slowly turns away from him. Readers often see the change as a metaphor for alienation, illness or being treated as useless once you can no longer earn money.
culture.ask: Have you ever felt like a different creature in a new job, school or country? What changed in how people treated you?

opts: He's a real black-horse candidate for the leadership.
He's a real dark-horse candidate for the leadership.
He's a real dark-pony candidate for the leadership.
bend.why: Dark horse works naturally as an adjective: a dark-horse candidate. The colour and animal are fixed.

opts: The report slaughters several sacred bulls of economic policy.
The report slaughters several holy cattle of economic policy.
The report slaughters several sacred cows of economic policy.
bend.why: Slaughtering sacred cows is a natural extension: challenging untouchable ideas.

opts: Honestly, there's a whole herd of elephants in this meeting.
Honestly, there's a whole herd of elephants on this meeting.
Honestly, there's an elephant inside the middle of this meeting.
bend.why: Joking that there's a herd of elephants extends the image naturally: many avoided problems.

talk: Orwell turned a farm into a political system. If you wrote a fable about your workplace or country, which animals would you use, and for whom?
Is there an elephant in the room in your profession or community that people avoid discussing? Keep it general if you prefer.
Role-play: you accidentally let the cat out of the bag about a colleague's resignation. Apologise to Bill, who plays the colleague.
Have you ever felt like a fish out of water? What helped you adapt?
Which animal metaphors from your language don't work in English? Which animal stands for stupidity, loyalty or cunning where you grew up?
